claim: Paranoia is the belief that harm is intended by others.
source: Paranoia is the belief that harm is intended by others.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract without supporting data or citations in this specific sentence.

claim: Paranoia may arise from selective pressures to infer and avoid social threats, particularly in ambiguous or changing circumstances.
source: It may arise from selective pressures to infer and avoid social threats, particularly in ambiguous or changing circumstances.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the evolutionary origins of paranoia, presented as a hypothesis without direct empirical support in this sentence.

claim: Uncertainty may be sufficient to elicit learning differences in paranoid individuals, without social threat.
source: We propose that uncertainty may be sufficient to elicit learning differences in paranoid individuals, without social threat.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, stated as a proposal to be tested.

claim: Paranoia is associated with a stronger prior on volatility.
source: Paranoia is associated with a stronger prior on volatility, accompanied by elevated sensitivity to perceived changes in the task environment.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the study's findings, supported by computational modeling results presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Paranoia is accompanied by elevated sensitivity to perceived changes in the task environment.
source: Paranoia is associated with a stronger prior on volatility, accompanied by elevated sensitivity to perceived changes in the task environment.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the study's findings, supported by computational modeling results.

claim: Methamphetamine exposure in rats recapitulates impaired uncertainty-driven belief updating.
source: Methamphetamine exposure in rats recapitulates this impaired uncertainty-driven belief updating and rigid anticipation of a volatile environment.
evidence: This is a summary claim of findings from the rat experiment, supported by computational modeling results.

claim: Methamphetamine exposure in rats recapitulates rigid anticipation of a volatile environment.
source: Methamphetamine exposure in rats recapitulates this impaired uncertainty-driven belief updating and rigid anticipation of a volatile environment.
evidence: This is a summary claim of findings from the rat experiment, supported by computational modeling results.

claim: Paranoia manifests along a continuum of increasing severity.
source: It manifests along a continuum of increasing severity (Freeman et al., 2005; Freeman et al., 2010; Freeman et al., 2011; Bebbington et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Fleeting paranoid thoughts prevail in the general population.
source: Fleeting paranoid thoughts prevail in the general population (Freeman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Freeman, 2006.

claim: Nearly 20% of individuals believed people were against them at times in the past year.
source: A survey of over 7000 individuals found that nearly 20% believed people were against them at times in the past year; approximately 8% felt people had intentionally acted to harm them (Freeman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a survey study by Freeman et al., 2011.

claim: Approximately 8% of individuals felt people had intentionally acted to harm them in the past year.
source: A survey of over 7000 individuals found that nearly 20% believed people were against them at times in the past year; approximately 8% felt people had intentionally acted to harm them (Freeman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a survey study by Freeman et al., 2011.

claim: Delusions of persecution occur in nearly 90% of first episode psychosis patients.
source: These delusions occur in nearly 90% of first episode psychosis patients (Freeman, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Freeman, 2007.

claim: Methamphetamine evokes new paranoid ideation particularly after repeated exposure or escalating doses (86% and 68%, respectively, in a survey of methamphetamine users).
source: Methamphetamine evokes new paranoid ideation particularly after repeated exposure or escalating doses (86% and 68%, respectively, in a survey of methamphetamine users) (Leamon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a survey study by Leamon et al., 2010.

claim: People who are paranoid have difficulties in laboratory tasks that require trust.
source: Sophisticated Game Theory driven approaches (such as the Dictator Game [Raihani and Bell, 2018; Raihani and Bell, 2017]) have largely re-described the phenomenon — people who are paranoid have difficulties in laboratory tasks that require trust (Raihani and Bell, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research using game theory approaches.

claim: Paranoid difficulties in trust tasks are not driven by personal threat per se, but by negative representations of others.
source: However, this is not driven by personal threat per se, but by negative representations of others (Raihani and Bell, 2018; Raihani and Bell, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raihani and Bell, 2018 and 2017.

claim: Negative representations of others in paranoia are learned.
source: We posit that such representations are learned (Fineberg et al., 2014; Behrens et al., 2008), via the same fundamental learning mechanisms (Cramer et al., 2002) that underwrite non-social learning in non-human species (Heyes and Pearce, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on learning mechanisms.

claim: Aberrations to domain-general learning mechanisms underlie paranoia.
source: We hypothesize that aberrations to these domain-general learning mechanisms underlie paranoia.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, stated explicitly.

claim: Expectations about the noisiness of the environment constrain whether we update beliefs or dismiss surprises as probabilistic anomalies.
source: Expectations about the noisiness of the environment constrain whether we update beliefs or dismiss surprises as probabilistic anomalies.
evidence: This is a statement about learning mechanisms, drawing on established knowledge in computational neuroscience.

claim: The higher the expected uncertainty, the less surprising an atypical outcome may be, and the less it drives belief updates.
source: The higher the expected uncertainty (i.e., 'I expect variable outcomes'), the less surprising an atypical outcome may be, and the less it drives belief updates ('this variation is normal').
evidence: This is a statement about learning mechanisms, drawing on established knowledge in computational neuroscience.

claim: Unexpected uncertainty describes perceived change in the underlying statistics of the environment.
source: Unexpected uncertainty, in contrast, describes perceived change in the underlying statistics of the environment (Yu and Dayan, 2005; Payzan-LeNestour and Bossaerts, 2011; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013) (i.e. 'the world is changing'), which may call for belief revision.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on uncertainty and learning.

claim: Excessive unexpected uncertainty is a signal of change.
source: Since excessive unexpected uncertainty is a signal of change, it might drive the recategorization of allies as enemies, which is a tenet of evolutionary theories of paranoia (Raihani and Bell, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the definition of unexpected uncertainty and evolutionary theories of paranoia.

claim: Excessive unexpected uncertainty might drive the recategorization of allies as enemies.
source: Since excessive unexpected uncertainty is a signal of change, it might drive the recategorization of allies as enemies, which is a tenet of evolutionary theories of paranoia (Raihani and Bell, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on evolutionary theories of paranoia, supported by a citation.

claim: The drive to flexibly recategorize associations extends to non-social, domain-general inferences.
source: We tested the hypothesis that this drive to flexibly recategorize associations extends to non-social, domain-general inferences.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Participants with paranoia expect the task to be volatile (high μ30).
source: Priors did not differ between groups at x2 (Table 3) but paranoid individuals and rats exposed to methamphetamine exhibited elevated μ30, they expected greater task volatility (Figure 2b, blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Participants with paranoia have expectations about task volatility that are more rigid (low ω3).
source: In summary, our modeling analyses suggest the following about paranoia in humans and methamphetamine exposed animals: they expect the task to be volatile (high μ30), their expectations about task volatility are more rigid (low ω3), and they confuse probabilistic errors and task volatility as a signal that the task has fundamentally changed (high κ, low ω2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Participants with paranoia confuse probabilistic errors and task volatility as a signal that the task has fundamentally changed (high κ, low ω2).
source: In summary, our modeling analyses suggest the following about paranoia in humans and methamphetamine exposed animals: they expect the task to be volatile (high μ30), their expectations about task volatility are more rigid (low ω3), and they confuse probabilistic errors and task volatility as a signal that the task has fundamentally changed (high κ, low ω2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: High paranoia subjects achieved fewer reversals than low paranoia subjects.
source: High paranoia subjects achieved fewer reversals (MD = −2.31, CI=[−4.504,–0.111,], t(30)=-2.145, p=0.04, Hedges' g = 0.798), but total points earned did not significantly differ, suggesting that there was no penalty for the different behaviors expressed by the more paranoid subjects (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1.

claim: Total points earned did not significantly differ between high and low paranoia subjects in Experiment 1.
source: High paranoia subjects achieved fewer reversals (MD = −2.31, CI=[−4.504,–0.111,], t(30)=-2.145, p=0.04, Hedges' g = 0.798), but total points earned did not significantly differ, suggesting that there was no penalty for the different behaviors expressed by the more paranoid subjects (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1.

claim: High paranoia participants earned fewer total points in Experiment 2.
source: Trial-by-trial reaction time did not differ significantly between low and high paranoia (Table 2), but high paranoia participants earned fewer total points (F(1, 299)=6.175, p=0.014, ηp2=0.020) and achieved fewer reversals (F(1, 299)=5.762, p=0.017, ηp2=0.019; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: High paranoia participants achieved fewer reversals in Experiment 2.
source: Trial-by-trial reaction time did not differ significantly between low and high paranoia (Table 2), but high paranoia participants earned fewer total points (F(1, 299)=6.175, p=0.014, ηp2=0.020) and achieved fewer reversals (F(1, 299)=5.762, p=0.017, ηp2=0.019; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: Choice switching after positive feedback (win-switch behavior) was elevated in high paranoia in Experiment 2.
source: Deck choice perseveration after negative feedback (lose-stay behavior) did not significantly differ by paranoia group, but choice switching after positive feedback (win-switch behavior) was elevated in high paranoia (block 1: F(1, 299)=7.117, p=0.008, ηp2=0.023; block 2: F(1, 299)=9.918, p=0.002, ηp2=0.032; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: Rats exposed to methamphetamine exhibited increased win-switch behavior.
source: Relative to rats exposed to saline, those rats exposed to methamphetamine exhibited increased win-switch behavior, similar to what we has observed in the high paranoia human participants, and additionally, unlike humans, they perseverated after negative feedback (Groman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Groman et al., 2018, which is re-analyzed in the current study.

claim: Rats exposed to methamphetamine perseverated after negative feedback.
source: Relative to rats exposed to saline, those rats exposed to methamphetamine exhibited increased win-switch behavior, similar to what we has observed in the high paranoia human participants, and additionally, unlike humans, they perseverated after negative feedback (Groman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Groman et al., 2018, which is re-analyzed in the current study.

claim: In Experiment 1, μ30 differed between high and low paranoia in both blocks.
source: In Experiment 1, we observed an interaction between task block and paranoia group (F(1, 30)=5.344, p=0.028, ηp2=0.151; Table 1): μ30 differed between high and low paranoia in both blocks (block 1, F(1, 30)=4.232, p=0.048, ηp2=0.124, MD = 0.658, CI=[0.005,1.312]; block 2, F(1, 30)=7.497, p=0.010, ηp2=0.20, MD = 1.598, CI=[0.406, 2.789]), but only low paranoia subjects significantly updated their priors between block 1 and block 2 (F(1, 30)=39.841, p=5.85E-07, ηp2=0.570, MD = 1.504, CI=[1.017, 1.99]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiment 1.

claim: Only low paranoia subjects significantly updated their μ30 priors between block 1 and block 2 in Experiment 1.
source: In Experiment 1, we observed an interaction between task block and paranoia group (F(1, 30)=5.344, p=0.028, ηp2=0.151; Table 1): μ30 differed between high and low paranoia in both blocks (block 1, F(1, 30)=4.232, p=0.048, ηp2=0.124, MD = 0.658, CI=[0.005,1.312]; block 2, F(1, 30)=7.497, p=0.010, ηp2=0.20, MD = 1.598, CI=[0.406, 2.789]), but only low paranoia subjects significantly updated their priors between block 1 and block 2 (F(1, 30)=39.841, p=5.85E-07, ηp2=0.570, MD = 1.504, CI=[1.017, 1.99]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiment 1.

claim: Paranoid participants and methamphetamine exposed rats updated stimulus-outcome associations more strongly in response to perceived volatility.
source: Paranoid participants and methamphetamine exposed rats updated stimulus-outcome associations more strongly in response to perceived volatility (e.g., correctly or incorrectly inferred reversals; Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 2b.

claim: κ showed significant paranoia group effects across the in laboratory experiment and online version 3.
source: κ showed significant paranoia group and block effects across the in laboratory experiment and online version 3 (Table 1; paranoia effects, in laboratory: F(1, 30)=7.599, p=0.010, ηp2=0.202, MD = 0.081, CI=[0.021, 0.140]; online version 3: F(1, 70)=13.521, p=0.0005, ηp2=0.162, MD = 0.068, CI=[0.031–0.104]; MDMETA = 0.079, CI=[0.063, 0.095], zMETA = 9.502 p=2.067E-21); see Table 3 for block effects).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: κ increased from baseline in rats on methamphetamine.
source: κ increased from baseline in rats on methamphetamine, yielding significant effects of treatment (F(1, 15)=13.356, p=0.002, ηp2=0.471, MD = 0.045, CI=[0.019, 0.072]) and time (F(1, 15)=9.132, p=0.009, ηp2=0.378, MD = 0.041, CI=[0.012, 0.069]); however, the interaction between time and treatment did not reach statistical significance (Table 3; Pre-Rx m = 0.499 [0.015] saline, 0.523 [0.040] methamphetamine; Post-Rx: m = 0.518 [0.053] saline, 0.585 [0.029] methamphetamine).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiment 3.

claim: Expected uncertainty (ω2) was decreased in paranoid participants and rats exposed to methamphetamine.
source: Expected uncertainty (ω2) was decreased in paranoid participants and rats exposed to methamphetamine (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 2b.

claim: Meta-volatility learning (ω3) was similarly decreased across paranoia and methamphetamine exposed groups.
source: Meta-volatility learning (ω3) was similarly decreased across paranoia and methamphetamine exposed groups (in laboratory, online version 3, and rats: MDMETA = −1.155, CI=[−2.139,–0.171], zMETA = −2.3, p=0.021), suggesting more reliance on expected task volatility (i.e., anticipated frequency of reversal events) than on actual task feedback.
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analytic results of computational modeling parameters.

claim: Win-switching was the prominent behavioral feature of both paranoid participants and rats exposed to methamphetamine.
source: Win-switching was the prominent behavioral feature of both paranoid participants and rats exposed to methamphetamine (Table 1, Table 2; Groman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from Experiments 1, 2, and 3.

claim: Paranoid participants exhibited elevated choice stochasticity (U-values) across task blocks.
source: Across task blocks, paranoid participants exhibited elevated choice stochasticity (paranoia by version interaction, F(3, 298)=3.438, p=0.017, ηp2=0.033; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: Choice stochasticity in paranoid participants was specific to versions with contingency transition.
source: Post-hoc tests indicate that this stochasticity was specific to versions with contingency transition, suggesting a relationship to unexpected uncertainty (Figure 3b; version 3, F(1, 298)=17.585, p=3.6E-5, ηp2=0.056, MD = 0.071, CI=[0.038, 0.104]; version 4, F(1, 298)=6.397, p=0.012, ηp2=0.021, MD = 0.039, CI=[0.009, 0.07]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: The HGF model recapitulated elevated win-switch behavior in simulated paranoid participants.
source: Using individually estimated HGF parameters to generate ten simulations per participant, we recapitulated both elevated win-switch behavior (paranoia effect, F(1, 70)=15.394, p=2.01E-4, ηp2=0.180, MD = 0.186, CI=[0.091, 0.28]) and choice stochasticity (U-value; paranoia effect, F(1, 70)=13.362, p=0.0005, ηp2=0.160, MD = 0.065, CI=[0.030, 0.101]) in simulated paranoid participants (Figure 7b; simulated win-switch rate, low paranoia: m = 0.24 [0.02], high paranoia: m = 0.43 [0.04]; simulated U-value, low paranoia: m = 0.851 [0.008], high paranoia: m = 0.916 [0.016]).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results using the HGF model.

claim: The HGF model recapitulated elevated choice stochasticity in simulated paranoid participants.
source: Using individually estimated HGF parameters to generate ten simulations per participant, we recapitulated both elevated win-switch behavior (paranoia effect, F(1, 70)=15.394, p=2.01E-4, ηp2=0.180, MD = 0.186, CI=[0.091, 0.28]) and choice stochasticity (U-value; paranoia effect, F(1, 70)=13.362, p=0.0005, ηp2=0.160, MD = 0.065, CI=[0.030, 0.101]) in simulated paranoid participants (Figure 7b; simulated win-switch rate, low paranoia: m = 0.24 [0.02], high paranoia: m = 0.43 [0.04]; simulated U-value, low paranoia: m = 0.851 [0.008], high paranoia: m = 0.916 [0.016]).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results using the HGF model.

claim: κ was the only parameter whose main effect of paranoia and paranoia-by-version interaction survived covariation for demographic, mental health and cognitive covariates.
source: Thus κ – participants' perception of unexpected uncertainty – was the only parameter whose main effect of paranoia (higher κ in high paranoia participants) and paranoia-by-version interaction (higher κ in high paranoia participants as a function of increasing unexpected volatility in version 3) survived covariation for demographic, mental health and cognitive covariates.
evidence: This claim is supported by ANCOVA results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Paranoia was a significant predictor of κ in multiple regression analysis.
source: Paranoia was a significant predictor of κ (β = 0.343, t = 2.470, p=0.016, CI=[0.012, 0.113]) but depression and anxiety were not (BDI: β = 0.086, t = 0.423, p=0.674, CI=[−0.043, 0.066]; BAI: β = −0.043, t = −0.218, p=0.828, CI=[−0.063, 0.050]).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple regression analysis results.

claim: Depression and anxiety were not significant predictors of κ in multiple regression analysis.
source: Paranoia was a significant predictor of κ (β = 0.343, t = 2.470, p=0.016, CI=[0.012, 0.113]) but depression and anxiety were not (BDI: β = 0.086, t = 0.423, p=0.674, CI=[−0.043, 0.066]; BAI: β = −0.043, t = −0.218, p=0.828, CI=[−0.063, 0.050]).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple regression analysis results.

claim: Two-step cluster analysis identified two clusters with good cohesion and separation based on μ30, κ, ω2, and ω3.
source: We identified two clusters with good cohesion and separation, meaning that subjects sorted into two groups (each containing rodents and humans) whose parameters travelled in such a way that their values were close to the centroid or mean of the cluster they were in and as far as possible from the centroid of the other cluster (average silhouette coefficient = 0.7; cluster size ratio = 2.46; Figure 9a).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster analysis results.

claim: Cluster one membership was significantly associated with high paranoia and methamphetamine exposure.
source: Cluster one membership was significantly associated with high paranoia and methamphetamine exposure, χ2(1, n = 121)=29.447, p=5.75E-8, Cramer's V = 0.493 (Figure 9c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cluster membership.

claim: The cluster solution did not separate rats from humans.
source: Importantly, the cluster solution did not separate rats from humans (despite the differences in task structure, incentives, manipulanda, and phylogeny).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster analysis results.

claim: Unexpected uncertainty and the κ parameter of the HGF are thought to be signaled via the locus coeruleus and noradrenaline.
source: Unexpected uncertainty, and the κ parameter of the HGF in particular (Marshall et al., 2016), are thought to be signaled via the locus coeruleus and noradrenaline (Yu and Dayan, 2005; Payzan-LeNestour and Bossaerts, 2011; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013; Tervo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the neural mechanisms of uncertainty.

claim: The locus coeruleus and noradrenaline are thought to modulate switching versus staying behaviors.
source: This mechanism is thought to modulate switching versus staying behaviors (Kane et al., 2017; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Aston-Jones et al., 1999; Eldar et al., 2013), as well as responses to stress (Borodovitsyna et al., 2018; McCall et al., 2015; Atzori et al., 2016) and subliminal fear cues (Liddell et al., 2005) to coordinate fight-or-flight responses (Atzori et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the locus coeruleus and noradrenaline.

claim: Methamphetamine may induce dysfunction in the locus coeruleus and noradrenaline system.
source: Methamphetamine may induce similar dysfunction (Ferrucci et al., 2019; Ferrucci et al., 2013; Ferrucci et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on methamphetamine effects.

claim: Acute moderate doses of methamphetamine increase pre-synaptic catecholamine release, particularly noradrenaline.
source: Acute moderate doses increase pre-synaptic catecholamine release, particularly noradrenaline (Rothman et al., 2001), and induce exploratory locomotive effects modulated through adrenoceptors on dopamine neurons (Ferrucci et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on methamphetamine pharmacology.

claim: Excessive release of noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus into the anterior cingulate cortex drives feedback insensitivity and stochastic switching behavior in rats.
source: Excessive release of noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus into the anterior cingulate cortex drives feedback insensitivity and stochastic switching behavior in rats completing a three-option counter prediction task (Tervo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tervo et al., 2014.

claim: Behavioral stochasticity impedes predators' abilities to create accurate, actionable countermeasures.
source: As a protean defense mechanism, behavioral stochasticity impedes predators' abilities to create accurate, actionable countermeasures (Humphries and Driver, 1970; Richardson et al., 2018; Humphries and Driver, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on protean defense mechanisms.

claim: Aberrant mismatches between expected and experienced sensory consequences of actions can lead to the misattribution of one's movements to an external agent.
source: Aberrant mismatches between expected and experienced sensory consequences of actions, weighted by their uncertainty (Wolpert and Ghahramani, 2000), can lead to the misattribution of one's movements to an external agent (Blakemore et al., 2000; Blakemore et al., 1998; Blakemore et al., 1999; Blakemore et al., 2002; Frith et al., 2000a; Frith et al., 2000b; Shergill et al., 2005; Shergill et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on efference copy models and psychosis.

claim: When humans experience non-social volatility, they appeal to the influence of powerful enemies.
source: When humans experience non-social volatility, (For example through threats to their sense of control [Whitson and Galinsky, 2008] or exposure to surprising non-social stimuli [Proulx et al., 2012; Heine et al., 2006]), they appeal to the influence of powerful enemies, even when those enemies' influence is not obviously linked to the volatility (Sullivan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on responses to volatility.

claim: Approximately two-thirds of participants endorsed three or fewer items on the SCID-II paranoid personality subscale in Experiment 1.
source: Approximately two-thirds of participants endorsed three or fewer items on the SCID-II paranoid personality subscale (median = 1 item).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from Experiment 1.

claim: Participants who endorsed four or more items on the SCID-II paranoid personality subscale were classified as high paranoia.
source: Participants who endorsed four or more items were classified as high paranoia (n = 11), consistent with the diagnostic threshold for paranoid personality disorder.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how participants were classified.

claim: Diagnostic category was significantly associated with paranoia group membership in Experiment 1.
source: Diagnostic category (i.e., healthy control, mood disorder, or schizophrenia spectrum) was significantly associated with paranoia group membership, χ2 (2, n = 32)=12.329, p=0.002, Cramer's V = 0.621, as was psychiatric medication usage, χ2 (1, n = 32)=9.871, p=0.003, Cramer's V = 0.555.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of demographic data from Experiment 1.

claim: Psychiatric medication usage was significantly associated with paranoia group membership in Experiment 1.
source: Diagnostic category (i.e., healthy control, mood disorder, or schizophrenia spectrum) was significantly associated with paranoia group membership, χ2 (2, n = 32)=12.329, p=0.002, Cramer's V = 0.621, as was psychiatric medication usage, χ2 (1, n = 32)=9.871, p=0.003, Cramer's V = 0.555.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of demographic data from Experiment 1.

claim: Paranoia, BAI, and BDI scores were significantly elevated in the high paranoia group relative to low paranoia controls in Experiment 1.
source: As expected, paranoia, BAI, and BDI scores were significantly elevated in the high paranoia group relative to low paranoia controls (Table 1; paranoia: mean difference (MD) = 0.536, CI=[0.455,0.618], t(30)=13.476, p=2.92E-14, Hedges' g = 5.016; BAI: MD = 0.585, CI=[0.239, 0.931], t(30)=3.453, p=0.002, Hedges' g = 1.285, MD = −0.585; BDI: MD = 0.427, CI=[0.078, 0.775], t(11.854) = 2.67, p=0.021, Hedges' g = 1.255).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of questionnaire data from Experiment 1.

claim: Participants' demographic and mental health questionnaire responses did not differ significantly across task version experiments in Experiment 2.
source: Participants' demographic and mental health questionnaire responses did not differ significantly across task version experiments (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of demographic data from Experiment 2.

claim: Total points and reversals achieved suggest variations in task difficulty across task versions in Experiment 2.
source: Total points and reversals achieved suggest variations in task difficulty (Table 2, version effects: points earned, F(3, 299)=32.288, p=4.16E-18, ηp2=0.245; reversals achieved, F(3, 299)=4.329, p=0.005, ηp2=0.042), but there was no significant association between task version and attrition rate (52.7%, 52.9%, 54.6%, and 53.1% attrition, respectively; χ2 (3, n = 752)=0.167, p=0.983, Cramer's V = 0.015).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: There was no significant association between task version and attrition rate in Experiment 2.
source: Total points and reversals achieved suggest variations in task difficulty (Table 2, version effects: points earned, F(3, 299)=32.288, p=4.16E-18, ηp2=0.245; reversals achieved, F(3, 299)=4.329, p=0.005, ηp2=0.042), but there was no significant association between task version and attrition rate (52.7%, 52.9%, 54.6%, and 53.1% attrition, respectively; χ2 (3, n = 752)=0.167, p=0.983, Cramer's V = 0.015).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of attrition data from Experiment 2.

claim: Paranoia group effects were specific to versions of the task in which we explicitly manipulated uncertainty via contingency transition.
source: Paranoia group effects were specific to versions of the task in which we explicitly manipulated uncertainty via contingency transition which increased volatility (Figure 3, Table 5, versions 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiment 2.

claim: Paranoia by version interactions were observed for κ and ω2 in Experiment 2.
source: Specifically, we observed paranoia by version interactions for κ (F(3, 299)=4.178, p=0.006, ηp2=0.040) and ω2 (F(3, 299)=2.809, p=0.040, ηp2=0.027; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiment 2.

claim: Significant paranoia group effects for κ were restricted to version 3 in Experiment 2.
source: Post-hoc tests confirmed that significant paranoia group effects were restricted to version 3 (κ: F(1, 299)=12.230, p=0.001, ηp2=0.039, MD = 0.068, CI=[0.03,0.106]; ω2: F(1, 299)=8.734, p=0.003, ηp2=0.028, MD = −0.993, CI=[−1.655,–0.332]) and a trend for version 4 (ω2: F(1, 299)=2.909, p=0.089, ηp2=0.010, MD = −0.528, CI=[−1.138, 0.081], Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiment 2.

claim: Significant paranoia group effects for ω2 were restricted to version 3 in Experiment 2.
source: Post-hoc tests confirmed that significant paranoia group effects were restricted to version 3 (κ: F(1, 299)=12.230, p=0.001, ηp2=0.039, MD = 0.068, CI=[0.03,0.106]; ω2: F(1, 299)=8.734, p=0.003, ηp2=0.028, MD = −0.993, CI=[−1.655,–0.332]) and a trend for version 4 (ω2: F(1, 299)=2.909, p=0.089, ηp2=0.010, MD = −0.528, CI=[−1.138, 0.081], Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of computational modeling results from Experiment 2.

claim: The paranoia by version interaction for κ remained robust across all three ANCOVAs (demographics, mental health, cognitive).
source: For κ, our metric of unexpected uncertainty, the paranoia by version interaction remained robust across all three ANCOVAs (demographics: F(3, 294)=3.753, p=0.011, ηp2=0.037; mental health: F(3, 257)=4.417, p=0.005, ηp2=0.049; cognitive: F(3, 290)=4.304, p=0.005 ηp2=0.043).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANCOVA results from Experiment 2.

claim: The paranoia by version interaction for ω2 was robust to mental health and cognitive factors.
source: The paranoia by version interaction for ω2 was robust to mental health and cognitive factors (F(3, 257)=3.617, p=0.014, ηp2=0.041; F(3, 290)=3.017, p=0.030, ηp2=0.030).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANCOVA results from Experiment 2.

claim: κ group effects survived FDR corrections within each experiment.
source: κ group effects survived corrections within each experiment (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by FDR correction analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: μ30 group effects survived FDR correction for experiment 1.
source: In addition to κ, μ30 survived for experiment 1; μ30 and ω2 survived in online version 3; and μ30, ω2, and ω3 survived in experiment three as group effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by FDR correction analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: μ30 and ω2 group effects survived FDR correction in online version 3.
source: In addition to κ, μ30 survived for experiment 1; μ30 and ω2 survived in online version 3; and μ30, ω2, and ω3 survived in experiment three as group effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by FDR correction analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: μ30, ω2, and ω3 group effects survived FDR correction in experiment three.
source: In addition to κ, μ30 survived for experiment 1; μ30 and ω2 survived in online version 3; and μ30, ω2, and ω3 survived in experiment three as group effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by FDR correction analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: The correlation between paranoia and κ in the first block of the task increases when analyses are restricted to individuals with paranoia scores greater than 0.
source: The correlation between paranoia and κ in the first block of the task increases from r = 0.3, p=0.011, CI=[0.074, 0.497] (all participants, n = 72) to r = 0.588, p=8.0E-5, CI=[0.335, 0.762] (participants with paranoia >0, n = 39).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of data from online version 3.

claim: Paranoia predicts kappa across participants, while anxiety and depression do not.
source: Thus, paranoia predicts kappa across participants. Anxiety and depression do not predict kappa.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple regression analysis results.

claim: The model successfully simulates the key features of paranoid behavior: higher win-switching and stochastic choice.
source: Thus, the model we chose, with meta-volatility and three coupled layers of belief, successfully simulates the key features of paranoid behavior: higher win-switching and stochastic choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results using the HGF model.

claim: A Q-learning model with separate parameter weights for positive and negative prediction errors failed to capture paranoia group differences.
source: Fitting this model to online version 3, we saw no significant paranoia group differences in learning rates for positive or negative prediction errors in parameters derived from all 180 trials (independent samples t-test: α+, t(70)=-0.532, p=0.597; α-, t(70)=0.963, p=0.339), nor did we see any significant block*paranoia or paranoia group effects by repeated measures ANOVA (block*paranoia: α+, F(1, 70)=0.188, p=0.732, α-, F(1, 70)=0.378, p=0.540; paranoia group: α+, F(1, 70)=0.243, p=0.623, α-, F(1, 70)=1.292, p=0.260).
evidence: This claim is supported by alternative model fitting results.

claim: A simpler two-level HGF model failed to capture paranoia group differences.
source: This model failed to capture the task effects or group differences in its parameters (see Table 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by alternative model fitting results.

claim: Elevated win-switch tendencies have been reported in youths with bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and anxiety disorder.
source: However, elevated win-switch tendencies have been reported in youths with bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and anxiety disorder (Dickstein et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dickstein et al., 2010.

claim: A prior study in people with schizophrenia described excessive win-switch behavior that correlated with the severity of delusional beliefs and hallucinations.
source: A prior study in people with schizophrenia described excessive win-switch behavior that correlated with the severity of delusional beliefs and hallucinations (Waltz, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Waltz, 2017.

claim: An elevated prior on environmental volatility (μ30) and higher sensitivity to this volatility (κ) have been observed in HGF analyses of 2-choice probabilistic reversal-learning in medicated and unmedicated patients with schizophrenia.
source: Likewise, an elevated prior on environmental volatility (μ30) and higher sensitivity to this volatility (κ) have been observed in HGF analyses of 2-choice probabilistic reversal-learning in medicated and unmedicated patients with schizophrenia (Deserno, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deserno, 2018.

claim: Lesions of the mediodorsal thalamus in non-human primates engender win-switching behavior.
source: Lesions of the mediodorsal thalamus in non-human primates (Chakraborty et al., 2016) or neurons projecting from the amygdala to orbitofrontal cortex in rats (Groman et al., 2019) engender win-switching.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chakraborty et al., 2016.

claim: Lesions of neurons projecting from the amygdala to orbitofrontal cortex in rats engender win-switching behavior.
source: Lesions of the mediodorsal thalamus in non-human primates (Chakraborty et al., 2016) or neurons projecting from the amygdala to orbitofrontal cortex in rats (Groman et al., 2019) engender win-switching.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Groman et al., 2019.
